_comment: Hand corrections layered over the OCR seed by tools/build_coords.py.
Board coordinates are pixels of .build/a11/drawing_full.png (5880 x 3340);
schematic coordinates are pixels of the matching sch<n>_full.png. A11's six
sheets were each cropped separately and no two are the same size, so
sheetImageSize carries one entry per sheet.
A11's drawing reads well -- the silkscreen is clear of the component
outlines -- but the reader still mis-attributed 57 of its 243 markers, almost
all of them a label read as a neighbouring designator: C100 on C106's label,
R28 on VR28's, U8 on Q8's, C16 on C19's. Every board marker was rendered and
looked at; the 57 wrong ones were replaced by a hand position where the real
silkscreen could be found and dropped where it could not.
171 positions here were measured off a gridded crop of drawing_full.png and
then re-rendered and checked one by one before being kept.
The six sheets were reviewed the same way, marker by marker, and they fared
far worse than the board: of 506 machine reads, 245 were right. A schematic
is mostly text that is not a designator, so the reader places markers on pin
names, bus labels, zone references, part numbers, captions and title blocks
with the same confidence it places real ones. Sheet 6, the microprocessor
interface, kept 33 of 86. What survived is recorded by omission -- anything
not in dropSchematic below was looked at and kept.
_boardComment: x,y are the marker centre in drawing_full.png pixels; w,h its size.
All twelve test points are placed here rather than taken from OCR, because a
test point's marker has to sit on what you probe. A11 prints them in one row
along the top edge of the board, each as vertical text reading bottom to top.
Six of them -- TP1 TP3 TP8 TP9 TP10 TP12 -- carry a short bar drawn directly
above the text: that bar is the wire loop, and those six are exactly the six
that have a line in the parts list (816090-style purchased loops). Their
markers span bar and label together. The other six -- TP2 TP4 TP5 TP6 TP7
TP11 -- have no line in the parts list and no pad drawn on the artwork at
all; they are plated eyelets, and their markers are the label only. That is
recorded per test point in 'note' so the distinction is not lost.

_dropComment: OCR hits confirmed wrong by rendering them on the drawing, and for which no
real silkscreen could be found to move them to.
A1 and A2 are the two SIP daughter boards (DAC FILTER and DAC BUFFERED
REFERENCE). Their markers sat on C102 and on Z5's outline. No 'A1' or 'A2'
silkscreen was found anywhere on the drawing in a full gridded sweep, so they
are in notOnDrawing rather than guessed at. Both outlines ARE on the drawing --
an unlabelled long narrow rectangle under HR5 and another under HR6 -- but the
drawing never says which is which, and nothing on it or on the sheets settles
that, so neither outline is claimed. Both are placed on their sheets, where
the blocks are captioned A11-1 and A11-2.
VR1's marker was a truncation of VR10. The real VR1 silkscreen does exist, at
the far right of the board beside T1 and C108; VR1 is placed there by hand and
is no longer dropped.
H1 (a screw) and H2 (a C-MOS handling form) have no silkscreen and move to
notOnDrawing; X1, a 40-pin IC socket, sits under its IC and is not labelled.
R128 is not dropped and not placed. It is a 200K 0805 chip resistor that
appears only in the 1996 parts list, and no R128 silkscreen was found on the
drawing: the R124..R127 column it would belong to ends at R127. Its one
machine read, on sheet 6, turned out to be R108's label. It is in notOnDrawing
rather than guessed at.
_notOnDrawingComment: Parts in the list of replaceable parts that carry no silkscreen designator on
the assembly drawing: screws, nuts, rivets, spacers, ejectors, heat sinks,
shields, moulded covers, the static bag and the C-MOS handling form. X1 is
the 40-pin IC socket, which is drawn only as the outline under its IC.
They stay in the parts list and remain searchable; there is simply nothing on
A1, A2 and R128 join them for a narrower reason. A1 and A2 are the two SIP
daughter boards; their outlines are drawn but carry no designator, and see
the drop comment above for why neither outline is claimed. R128 is a 200K
0805 chip resistor whose R124..R127 column on the drawing ends at R127 -- a
gridded sweep and a search of the artwork found no R128 anywhere.
_dropSchematicComment: Reads on a sheet that are not the designator they were taken for, dropped
per sheet. Three kinds dominate, and all three are visible once the sheet is
rendered rather than read as numbers:
1. The package pinout legend. Every A11 sheet carries a column of FRONT/TOP
package views captioned with the designators they apply to -- sheet 1's is
the whole right-hand column, 34 markers. The parts are real and are drawn
somewhere, but not there, so the marker is wrong while the name is right.
2. The test point legend table. TP1 = SCOM (PG1 C7) and so on: the table is
crisp text in a neat column and the reader prefers it to the flag symbol
on the net. The table's own zone references say which sheet each test
point really lives on, and only TP1 is on sheet 1.
3. Ordinary text read as a designator -- a net name (RLH COM as Z5, +5 FR1 as
X1), a part value (TIP120 as TP1, 10V as Q5), a word in a note (HR6 as H1,
REF HEATER as R7, WIRE LOOP TYPE as L7), a pin number (11 as T1).

_layersComment: Alignment of the photograph to board space. Thirty-six landmark pairs, each
one a designator whose silkscreen is legible in both images. Left column:
C19 and C20 at the top left, C57, Q14, CR2, Q19 and Q18 across the middle,
Z4, L10, Q15, Q24, Q17, Q23 and Q10 down to the bottom edge. Middle: C110,
hand column: Z10, C106, U31, U32, U36, R124 and the R104 corner.
This is the re-alignment against the covers-off photograph. The old shot had
the adc-amplifier shield (M2) over the Z10 block and a second shield over the
U25/U31 column, so there was no usable silkscreen right of x=0.80 and the fit
spanned the right-hand column instead of being anchored in it. Both shields
are off in this one: Z10, U25, U31, U35/U32/U36, U6, U7, U8, U9, the R124-127
row and the C101-C106 row are all legible, and seven of the landmarks now sit
in that column. The two moulded hybrid covers (MP1, MP31) are still fitted,
so HR5 and HR6 themselves remain unmeasurable -- their outlines and mounting
pads line up, but nothing inside them does -- and the K1-K8 relay block at
x 0.15-0.40, y 0.62-0.93 is relay lids rather than board, so that patch is
bracketed by landmarks rather than anchored inside.
The src side is not eyeballed: it is the reviewed board coordinate of that
designator from data/a11.coords.json, so it is the same point the markers
are drawn from. The dst side was not eyeballed either -- the locator
drawing is the silkscreen artwork, and the photograph shows that same
silkscreen in yellow ink, so the drawing patch around each designator was
cross-correlated against the photograph and each pair is a local
registration rather than a click on a pixel grid. The patch is taken from
the drawing's part outlines with the designator lettering stripped out,
because the drawing does not print the text where the board does.
Fit residuals are 0.2 to 4.9 px in the photograph (3400 px wide) at every
landmark but one; R104 sits 10.2 px out because it anchors the bottom-right
corner, which a single homography cannot reach without spoiling the rest.
Checked by warping the photograph into board space and drawing the locator
artwork over it: the DIP and leadless-carrier outlines, the relay bodies,
the toroid row along the bottom, the chip-part rows down the right-hand
column and the board edge all sit on their parts. Sampling the whole board
with the same correlation afterwards gives, over 421 patches, a median error
of 2.7 px and a 90th percentile of 5.0 px in the photograph. The worst region
is the empty bottom-right corner at about 10 px.
Marked approximate. The shot is not perfectly overhead, and the ejector
ears and the threaded standoffs stand proud of the board -- they show 15
to 20 px of parallax against the drawing and were deliberately not used
as landmarks, mechanical though they are. Only flat, in-plane silkscreen
was used. The drawing's own geometry is not projective either: its left
quarter needs about 20 px more x than a homography fitted to the rest of
the board gives it, so the fit is balanced across the two rather than
letting the dense middle win.
src is normalised in the drawing (3000 x 1704), dst in the photo
